1.pericope_label: Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.

schools.summary: Face the textual question at the outset. A decided preponderance of manuscript authority compels the reading let us have, though the older reading would seem to make the best sense, and a hortatory element is thereby introduced which does not naturally belong to the passage; suggest a very early copyist's error afterwards corrected by conjecture, noting that in the two oldest manuscripts the familiar reading appears as a correction. Or allow no hesitation: the subjunctive is the correct text beyond a doubt, and it is curious how perverse many real scholars have been on this phrase, one calling it difficult if not impossible to explain — the mode is volitive and the present expresses linear action, so the exhortation is not make peace, which the ingressive aorist would have meant, but keep on enjoying the peace already possessed. Then set out the chapter's design as showing the effects of a doctrine already established, listing the steps of the preceding argument. Note the rarity of the word for access, which occurs elsewhere only twice, and that grace is here a field into which we have been introduced and where we stand; and that the word rendered rejoice is the one used elsewhere for boasting, so that the Christian has his boasting though not on his own merits. Collect the parallel exhortations to glory in persecution, quote Bacon that prosperity is the blessing of the Old Testament and adversity of the New, and trace the phrase about not being ashamed to the psalm about fathers who trusted and were not confounded.

Insist that the access is a continuing privilege rather than a momentary one: we are not brought to God for the purpose of an interview but to remain with him, to be his household and by faith to behold his face and walk in the light of his countenance. Explain the word for patience as endurance under trial without loss or deterioration, a metaphor taken from the refining of metals, and add that they do not speak from any sudden raptures or extraordinary sensations of spiritual joy. Report the context of the objection, that the Jews urged the persecuted state of the Christians as inconsistent with being the Messiah's people, so that it is with great propriety that the apostle so often mentions the blessings arising from this very thing; and quote Theodoret that he says not we patiently endure afflictions but we rejoice in them.

Define the peace narrowly and test it against experience: it means tranquillity of conscience arising from feeling oneself reconciled to God, and whoever seeks that tranquillity by works labours in vain, since either his heart is asleep through disregard of God's judgment or else it is full of trembling and dread until it reposes on Christ, who alone is our peace. Call the whole chapter amplification calculated to explain as much as to confirm. Meet the obvious objection before drawing out the chain of tribulation: lest anyone scoff that Christians with all their glorying are strangely harassed in this life, answer that the calamities do not merely fail to prevent blessedness but promote the glorying — while adding that the saints are not free from dread or undistressed by bitterness, since there is no patience where there is no feeling of bitterness. Note that the style here is the prophets' rather than the ordinary Greek, the first two verses forming a pair of distichs in which the second restates the first and adds a clause; and distinguish two hopes in the passage, one hanging directly on God's testimony and the later one gathered from what the believer finds within.

debates.question: Should the first verse read we have peace or let us have peace?

sides.position: Let us have, since a decided preponderance of manuscript authority compels it — though the older reading makes the best sense, and a very early copyist's error afterwards corrected by conjecture is possible
Let us have, beyond a doubt; it is curious how perverse many real scholars have been here, and the volitive present means keep on enjoying the peace, not make peace
Tranquillity of conscience arising from feeling oneself reconciled to God, which no one seeking it by works ever attains
The subsidence of storm and the awakening of an ardent hope looking forward to a glorious future

debates.question: Are the two hopes in the passage the same?

sides.position: No: the first hangs directly on the testimony of God, the second is gathered from what the believer finds within, and is the fruit of experience rather than of faith
The hope does not disappoint because it derives its certainty from the consciousness of justifying love

outliers.note: Alone treats the disputed reading as settled beyond doubt and criticises named scholars for hesitating over it, resolving the difficulty by the force of the present tense rather than by any appeal to the manuscripts.
Alone has a note distinguishing two hopes in the passage, one hanging directly on the testimony of God and a later one gathered not from the word without but from the feeling of what passes within.

themes: being justified by faith, we have peace with God
the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts

6.pericope_label: For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly. For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die. But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

schools.summary: State the design of the comparison: it illustrates the love of God by setting it beside the highest human benevolence, since none would be willing to die for a man seeking to injure them, whereas Christ was willing to die for bitter foes. Then take up the distinction between righteous and good. Quote Lightfoot for all the difference in the world between them, shown from Plato and from Christian writers, and define it as a difference of sympathy, the righteous man being absolutely without it while the good man is beneficent and kind — so that even in the case of the kindly man courage is called for to make the supreme sacrifice. Or grant a slight distinction of the same sort, that to be righteous is to direct the will in obedience to an external standard while to be good is to have a natural benevolence of disposition, and then say the distinction is not insisted on here, the two words being used almost convertibly; canvass and reject also the readings that make the phrase neuter, meaning in a good cause, or give the word the special sense of benefactor. On the verb rendered commendeth, note that the English happily covers a double sense, since the Greek is used of things in the sense of prove or establish and of persons in the sense of recommend; and observe that the ground of the love was not that we were Jews or Greeks, rich or poor, righteous or good, but plain sinners.

Frame the section as a descent to the spring-head: the streams of privilege are very sweet, but run them up and the source is found in Christ's dying for us, so that everything comes flowing through that precious blood. Divide what follows into three — the persons died for, the precious fruits of his death, and the parallel between the two Adams. Then work the two descriptions of those persons separately: without strength means a condition not merely sad but one they were unable to help themselves out of, lost with no visible way open for recovery, which is why the help is said to come in due time, God's manner being to help at a dead lift so that his own power and grace may be the more magnified; and ungodly means not merely helpless and therefore likely to perish but guilty and therefore deserving to perish, not merely mean and worthless but vile and obnoxious to the holy God.

Take the connecting particle as affirmative rather than causal and paraphrase the whole: such an example is most rare among men, that one dies for a just man, though it may sometimes happen; but grant that, and still for an ungodly man none will be found willing to die — and this is what Christ has done. Argue that confirming is the sense of the verb rendered commendeth, because the object was not to excite our gratitude but to strengthen the trust and confidence of our souls; and that in this the love appears, that being not moved by love on our part he of his own good will first loved us. Note that those called sinners here are the wholly vicious and abandoned, as elsewhere in Scripture, and that this appears from the contrast with those who are justified. Add the material the rendering omits: the just is he who acts as justice requires, on the rabbinic formula about mine and thine, while the good is the kind and beneficent man whom Cicero described as one who does good to those he can.

Supply the rabbinic scheme of four classes distinguished by what men say about mine and thine — the just who render each his own, those who accommodate each other by borrowing and lending, the pious who give up all for a neighbour, and the impious who take all and give nothing — then ask who would die for one of the first class, since there is nothing amiable in his conduct to endear him so far. Say that God set the act of infinite mercy in the most conspicuous light, so as to recommend it to the notice and admiration of all, and that those it was shown to were neither righteous nor good but impious and wicked.

debates.question: Do righteous and good differ here?

sides.position: All the difference in the world, shown from Plato and Christian writers — a difference of sympathy, the righteous man being without it and the good man beneficent and kind
There is a slight distinction, but it is not insisted upon here; the two words are used almost convertibly
The just renders every man his due, on the rabbinic formula; the good gives up all for his neighbour

debates.question: What does the verb rendered commendeth mean?

sides.position: The English happily covers a double sense, of proving or establishing and of recommending
Confirming, since the object was not to excite gratitude but to strengthen the confidence of our souls
Setting the act in the most conspicuous light, to recommend it to the notice and admiration of all

outliers.note: Alone supplies the rabbinic scheme of four moral classes distinguished by what men say about mine and thine, and uses it to ask who would die for a man of the first class.
Alone omits the clause about the good man from his rendering altogether, so that the material has to be supplied by his editor, who adds the Ciceronian definition of the vir bonus.

themes: scarcely for a righteous man will one die
while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us

9.pericope_label: Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. And not only so, but we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement.

schools.summary: Put the argument shortest: it runs from the greater to the less, the great thing being the justification in Christ's blood, so that the final salvation is less of a mystery. Expand the reasoning — it is much more reasonable to expect the lesser thing because there are fewer obstacles in the way, since if God overcame everything standing between him and enemies, we have far more reason to expect protection now that we are friends; and being purchased by that blood bestows on us a value proportionate to the price of the redemption and is itself a pledge that what was so dearly bought will be kept. Measure the two intervals in the argument and find them unequal: the distance separating enmity from reconciliation is large and that separating reconciliation from salvation small, though a difference remains, reconciliation being the initial act and the removal of guilt while salvation is the end of the Christian career, the one specially due to the death and the other brought about rather by the continued agency of the risen Saviour. Mark the progression in the joy, since earlier the rejoicing was in tribulation and in hope of glory but here it is in God himself, in his existence and attributes — a characteristic of true piety, since the sinner finds no pleasure in him and deems him unqualified for universal empire. Note also that a word must be supplied from the previous verse and that the state described is active rather than passive.

Press the connection as a certainty rather than a probability: justification and salvation are inseparably joined, so that whoever is justified shall be saved. Explain the emphasis on his blood as marking a violent death by the effusion of blood, and not the blood of bulls and goats but of the Son of God, which is therefore efficacious. Read the following verse as an explanation of this one amplified by a comparison between life and death, glossing by his life as through him being alive at God's right hand, having every power committed to him and making intercession for us. Then raise the difficulty honestly: the apostle seems inconsistent with himself, since if the death of Christ was a pledge of the divine love toward us it is hard to see how we were at the same time enemies. On the joy in God, take it of God as our covenant Father in Christ, in his perfections as engaged on our side and glorified in our salvation, and in all his providential dispensations.

Stop the exposition to answer a theological objection: is there then wrath in God? Is not wrath a human passion, and how can a human passion be in God? Answer first by a counter-question, whether love is not equally a human passion, and then directly — wrath in man and love in man are human passions, but wrath in God is not a human passion, nor is love as it is in God, so that the inspired writers ascribe both to God only in an analogical sense. Then object to a word in the received version: it was certainly improper to translate the noun at the close as atonement rather than reconciliation, since the cognate verb means to reconcile and is so rendered everywhere else it occurs; the word does not here mean the sacrificial death but rather its effect, the removal of the enmity and the consequent thorough change of our state from enmity to friendship. Add that the enmity in every human heart usually goes unsuspected, one property of sin being to blind the understanding so that men do not know their own state.

sides.position: Wrath in man is a human passion, but wrath in God is not, nor is love as it is in God; both are ascribed to him only in an analogical sense
From wrath means from the divine wrath, or the wrath to come
From hell, from the punishment due to sin

debates.question: Should the closing noun be rendered atonement?

sides.position: No: it was certainly improper, since the cognate verb means to reconcile and is so rendered everywhere else; the word means the effect of the atonement, not the sacrificial death
Reconciliation is the initial act, the removal of guilt; salvation is the end of the Christian career

debates.question: How can we have been enemies if the death was a pledge of love?

sides.position: The apostle seems here inconsistent with himself, and the difficulty must be faced
The work was undertaken while we were enemies, and that is itself the pledge that it will be perfected

outliers.note: Alone breaks off the exposition to ask whether there is wrath in God and whether wrath is not a human passion, answering by a counter-question about love and then by the doctrine that both are ascribed to God analogically.

Alone objects to the received version’s use of atonement for the closing noun, arguing from the cognate verb and its rendering elsewhere that the word means the removal of enmity rather than the sacrificial death.

themes: much more then, being now justified by his blood
when we were enemies, we were reconciled

12.pericope_label: Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned: (For until the law sin was in the world: but sin is not imputed when there is no law. Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come.

schools.summary: Notice first that the sentence breaks off before its second half arrives: the clause about sin and death entering by one man ought to have been answered by one about grace and life entering by one man, but the rapidity with which ideas throng into the writer's brain breaks the even flow of the sentence, and instead of the second member he turns to problems about sin and death and starts over again three verses later. State the problem of the interval sharply: sin was in the world from Adam downwards as a matter of history, but why guilt, and why death, the punishment of guilt? The man before Moses sinned, yet could not rightly be condemned until there was a law telling him plainly the difference between right and wrong — and observe that the law of nature is left out of consideration here, since the apostle applies that argument to his contemporaries and does not throw its operation back into the primitive ages. Or answer differently, that sin was there before Moses because the Jews were like Gentiles who had the law of reason and conscience, and that what the law added was responsibility and guilt; gloss the verb for imputing as a commercial term found in inscriptions and papyri for entering an item to someone's account. Personify the reign of death and list what makes it terrible: it is absolute, there is no escape, it is universal over old and young alike, and it would be eternal were it not for the gospel. Admit that the point about the type is introduced in a rhetorically faulty way, and excuse it by a circumstance of composition, that the letter was dictated and probably never revised.

Draw the conclusion the passage is usually taken to support, that men are not subjected to death for their own personal transgressions but for the sin of Adam, since through his transgression all come into the world with the seeds of death and corruption superadded to their moral depravity. Set the argument out as four propositions: sin was in the world during the interval, law was not, the sins were therefore not imputed unto death since men transgressed no rule with death annexed, and yet death reigned. Apply the clause about those who had not sinned after the similitude to infants who never sinned as Adam did in their own persons, and read the two men as public persons and federal heads, one the fountain of sin and death by his offence and the other of righteousness and life by his free gift. Quote Theodoret for a reading of until the law that nobody else offers, that it means not until the beginning but until the end of the law, so that while the law reigned sin had power.

Account for the turn medically: as the best physicians take great pains to discover the source of diseases and go to the very fountain of the mischief, so the blessed Paul, having shown justification from the patriarch, from the Spirit and from the dying of Christ, now confirms it from things opposite, that is from death and sin, enquiring whence death came in and how it prevailed. Answer that question from the sin of one: he having once fallen, even those who had not eaten of the tree became mortal from him. Then report the disputed phrase about the time before the law, which some take of the period before the giving of the law — the days of Abel, of Noah, of Abraham, until Moses was born — and ask what the sin was in those days.

Explain why the comparison was needed: since Christ came to redeem us from the calamity into which Adam precipitated his posterity, we cannot see clearly what we have in Christ except by having what we lost in Adam set before us — but warn that all things on both sides are not similar, which is why an exception follows. Note that the incompleteness of the sentence sometimes renders it obscure, the second clause answering to the former not being expressed, and that the beginning of the verse has occasioned a vast number of conjectures both as to the connection and as to the corresponding clause.

debates.question: Why does the sentence break off?

sides.position: Because the rapidity with which ideas throng into the writer's brain breaks the even flow of the structure
Because he turns aside to problems about sin and death and starts the comparison over again three verses later
Because the incompleteness is a feature of the style; the beginning of the verse has occasioned a vast number of conjectures

debates.question: Why did death reign before the law was given?

sides.position: Because the pre-Mosaic man sinned but could not rightly be condemned until a law told him plainly the difference between right and wrong; the law of nature is left out of consideration
Because the Jews were like Gentiles who had the law of reason and conscience; the coming of the law increased responsibility and guilt
Because men are not subjected to death for their own transgressions but for Adam's
Because he having once fallen, even those who had not eaten of the tree became mortal from him

debates.question: What does until the law mean?

sides.position: Until the giving of the Mosaic law, the period of Abel, Noah and Abraham
Not until the beginning of the law but until its end, so that while the law reigned sin had power

outliers.note: Alone excuses the passage’s rhetorical awkwardness by a circumstance of composition, that the epistle was dictated and probably never revised by its author, quoting a scholar who asks the reader to picture the writer at work.
Alone reports a reading of until the law that takes it as until the END of the law rather than until its beginning, quoting Theodoret for it against every other voice in the chapter.

themes: by one man sin entered into the world
sin is not imputed when there is no law
death reigned from Adam to Moses

15.pericope_label: But not as the offence, so also is the free gift. For if through the offence of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many. And not as it was by one that sinned, so is the gift: for the judgment was by one to condemnation, but the free gift is of many offences unto justification. For if by one man’s offence death reigned by one; much more they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ.)

schools.summary: Set the contrast out as a table of parallels, pairing the persons of the action, the action itself, its character, the persons affected, and its proximate and ulterior effects, so that the differences are thrown into relief by the resemblances. Then press a translation point with doctrinal weight: throughout the passage the reading should be the one and the many rather than one and many, since the many means mankind generally — and quote Bentley that by this accurate version some hurtful mistakes about partial redemption and absolute reprobation would have been avoided. Or take the opposite view of the same words, holding it unnecessary to the argument that the many in each case correspond, since one relates to Adam and the other to Christ. Mark the successive points of contrast as they come, the first being that the evil flowed from the sin of one man and the benefit from the work of one man, the second that the evil consequences flowed from a single act of guilt while the favours had respect to many acts. Give the reason for the repeated much more, that as a God of love he delights more in showing mercy and pardon than in giving just punishment, so that the gift surpasses the sin. State the closing contrast as a matter of verdicts, the sentence from a single case ending in condemnation while the free gift, prompted by many sins, ends in acquittal.

Map the structure of the comparison: the fall and the free gift differ in amplitude, the two men differ in power, the reason for both is then subjoined, and the offence and the gift are afterwards compared first as to their effect and then as to their cause. Then insist on the surplus of the gift over the loss: the comparison will not hold good in every respect, because the gift bestows blessings far beyond the consequences of the offence which therefore have no relation to it — and this had to be said both to prevent mistakes about the consequences of the offence and about the extent of gospel grace, and because the main design was to prove that grace extends to all men not only so far as it takes off the consequence of the offence, that is death without promise of a resurrection, but also in the surplusage of blessings by which it stretches far beyond it. Personify death as reigning and known by the destruction of his subjects, and set against that a reign in life for those who receive, retain and improve the abundant grace offered.

Warn that the apostle does not state the points of difference minutely but rather forestalls errors into which we might otherwise fall, and that none of the repetitions lacks either a corresponding clause or at least an ellipsis — defects in a discourse, but not prejudicial to the majesty of that celestial wisdom, since it has so happened through God's providence that the highest mysteries are delivered in the garb of a humble style. Then draw a polemical conclusion from the difference between one offence and many: since guilt from a single offence issued in the condemnation of all while the gratuitous gift is efficacious to justify from many offences, it appears that their opinion is impious who taught that we recover nothing by Christ but freedom from original sin. Add that the many offences we are freed from include not only those committed before baptism but those by which the saints contract new guilt daily, on account of which they would be justly condemned were they not continually relieved by this grace; and set gift against judgment, the latter meaning strict justice and the former gratuitous pardon.

debates.question: Should it be many or the many?

sides.position: The many throughout, meaning mankind generally; by this accurate version some hurtful mistakes about partial redemption and absolute reprobation would have been avoided
It is not necessary to the argument that the many in each case correspond, since one relates to Adam and the other to Christ

debates.question: In what does the gift exceed the offence?

sides.position: In bestowing blessings far beyond the consequences of the offence, which therefore have no relation to it
In its source: the evil flowed from one act of guilt, the favours had respect to many acts
In freeing us from many offences, including those by which the saints contract new guilt daily — against those who taught that we recover nothing but freedom from original sin
In the verdict: the sentence from a single case ends in condemnation, the free gift prompted by many sins ends in acquittal

outliers.note: Alone lays the contrast out as a formal table of paired terms, and alone presses the article before many as a translation point on which doctrines of partial redemption and absolute reprobation have turned.
Alone turns the difference between one offence and many into a charge of impiety against those who taught that Christ recovers for us nothing but freedom from original sin.

themes: but not as the offence, so also is the free gift
the judgment was by one to condemnation
they which receive abundance of grace shall reign in life

18.pericope_label: Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life. For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound: That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord.

schools.summary: Treat the summing-up verse as elliptical and say how the gap should be filled: the supplied words for judgment came are somewhat too much of a paraphrase, and it is better to render simply the issue was, using the same phrase for the parallel clause. Note that the first phrase about all men matches the earlier verse and the second matches the qualified statement about those who receive. Then lay out the alternatives on the conjunction in the verse about the law: it is usual to explain it as final, expressing God's ultimate purpose, and one modern commentator does so, but Chrysostom explained it as expressing result, which is a proper use of the word, and on that reading the sense is that the trespass did in fact abound — the actual effect of the Mosaic law for the Jews and the necessary result of all prohibitions. Read the verse also as an answer to an imagined Jewish objection, that the law of Moses was meant to meet the evils introduced by Adam and so made this scheme unnecessary; the reply is that its effect was to increase rather than diminish those evils. Gloss the verb for entering as a graphic metaphor, the law coming in to the side of the sin already existing and joining forces with it, and correct the received version's threefold abound, since the original word differs in two of the three places. Mark the tenses at the close, an aorist indicative for the throne sin established and an aorist subjunctive for the throne grace might establish, and pass on the judgement that this full rhetorical close has almost the value of a doxology.

Print the Greek and render it word for word, then offer what anyone without a creed to serve would take from the context: as by one sin all men came into condemnation, so by one righteous act all men came unto justification of life. State flatly that the increase of sin was the consequence and not the design of the law's coming in. Take the verb for entering as coming in privily, on the strength of the only other place it occurs, and apply it to the temporary and limited use of that law; then supply the reason the law was needed for such a purpose, asking how the finer deviations from a straight line could be ascertained without applying a known straight edge. Define justification of life as that sentence of God by which a sinner under sentence of death is adjudged to life, and read the abounding of grace as extending not only to the remission of the sin Adam brought on us but of all our own, not only to remission but to the infusion of holiness, not only to deliverance from death but to admission to a life more excellent than the one lost by the fall.

Call the sentence defective and complete it by putting two words in the nominative, then distinguish the noun used from the ordinary word for righteousness, showing from three other places that it means what is adjudged right, so that here it answers to condemnation and means absolution or acquittal as the determination of a judge. On why the law came in, note that the subject depends on what was said before about sin existing prior to the law, which immediately raises the question what the law was given for; a longer digression not being suitable, the point is deferred and it is only said in passing that the law came between Adam and Christ. Then notice at the close that the order of words is deranged, and explain why: the simple contrast would have set righteousness against sin, but the apostle was not content to oppose contrary to contrary and adds grace, that he might print more deeply on the memory that the whole is to be ascribed not to our merit but to the kindness of God.

debates.question: Is the conjunction in the verse about the law final or ecbatic?

sides.position: Usually explained as final, expressing God's ultimate purpose; but Chrysostom explained it as expressing result, which is a proper use of the word
The increase of sin was the consequence and not the design of the law's coming in
The effect of the law was to increase rather than diminish the evils, which answers the Jewish plea that it was adapted to overcome them

debates.question: How should the verb for the law's entering be rendered?

sides.position: Coming in privily, on the strength of the only other place it occurs
It cannot be so rendered here; it means simply that the law came in between Adam and Christ
Came in to the side of the sin already existing and joined forces with it

debates.question: How should the elliptical summing-up verse be completed?

sides.position: By supplying judgment came, which is implied though not in the Greek
Not so: those words are too much of a paraphrase, and the issue was is better
By putting two words in the nominative; and the noun used means not righteousness but what is adjudged right, that is acquittal

outliers.note: Alone reports both readings of the conjunction and attributes the result-reading to Chrysostom against a named modern who takes it as purpose, without finally deciding between them.

Alone prints the Greek of the verse in full and offers his own literal rendering, prefacing it with the remark that this is how anyone with no particular creed to serve would most probably understand it.

themes: by the righteousness of one, the free gift came upon all men
the law entered, that the offence might abound
where sin abounded, grace did much more abound
